title: Ryan Daniels — Crosby (legal services in the age of AI)
author: Ryan Daniels

dom.t: AI contracting: Deal velocity can undermine negotiation

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: Daniels does not substantively assess selective in-house insourcing or declining outside instructions. Instead, he shifts the emphasis to buyers’ continuing demand for trusted advisers and to AI-enabled legal delivery that still relies heavily on skilled lawyers.
qs: In other words, when people have some sort of legal issue, their instinct is to go to a trusted advisor.
And so it was obvious that we just had to get rid of that attempt and just double down on high-skill legal talent and really leveraging them.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: Daniels accepts that practical legal AI depends on expert-designed workflows, evaluation data and client-specific preferences rather than model output alone. He materially extends the proposition with a proposed agentic negotiation workflow that preserves an auditable trail and hands judgment-dependent “taste” issues back to human lawyers, while acknowledging that contract redlining and negotiation remain technically difficult and evidence is limited.
qs: So, if I know all the things you care about in a negotiation, when you're buying my software and I know all the things I care about, to just like simulate and show me an auditable trail of I would have asked for this and you'd responded with that, then I would have asked for this.
No, like at that point, then the human lawyers come in and then they talk through all those taste issues.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Daniels accepts the cluster’s core claim that AI cannot substitute for experience-dependent legal judgment and adds concrete operational evidence: Crosby’s lower-skilled staffing model failed its quality bar, while experienced lawyers were more productive with the same basic AI tools. This strengthens the competence-paradox and staffing arguments, though it does not address how apprenticeship should be reconstructed.
qs: And it was obvious at that point that our thesis was wrong because the other lawyer and I  who had a bit more legal experience, we were way more productive with just like the basic AI tools we built back then.
Whereas like the folks that we were onboarding, we weren't really seeing the quality improvements from AI that we were hoping to get.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Daniels accepts the value of workflow-focused AI used with experienced lawyers and materially extends the cluster through Crosby’s operational experience: attempts to use AI to uplift cheaper legal labour did not meet its quality bar, while experienced lawyers became more productive. Crosby also develops the copilot thesis into an AI-first legal-services model, with proposed agentic negotiation remaining prospective and human lawyers retained for judgment-sensitive issues.
qs: And it was obvious at that point that our thesis was wrong because the other lawyer and I  who had a bit more legal experience, we were way more productive with just like the basic AI tools we built back then.
No, like at that point, then the human lawyers come in and then they talk through all those taste issues.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Daniels accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI will reorganise legal production and pricing while preserving lawyers’ role in consequential judgment. Crosby’s operating experience materially develops that proposition by linking experienced-lawyer augmentation, integrated service delivery and per-piece pricing to the gradual transfer of routine work to AI agents, while acknowledging that autonomous negotiation remains aspirational.
qs: And the way we thought we could do that  is by getting rid of a billable hour, because if you think about it, if you do 10 tasks in an hour, 100 tasks in an hour, you're still billing an hour.
So like  you need a lawyer with some judgment on what is a court going to say in five years and we want it to get it right today.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Daniels accepts the cluster’s core view that legal AI selectively augments rather than broadly replaces lawyers, and materially extends it with Crosby’s operating experiment: experienced lawyers achieved greater productivity with AI, while lower-skilled workers did not achieve the expected quality gains. Crosby consequently redesigned staffing around high-skill lawyers, while acknowledging that the resulting model remains unfinished and operationally difficult to scale.
qs: And it was obvious at that point that our thesis was wrong because the other lawyer and I  who had a bit more legal experience, we were way more productive with just like the basic AI tools we built back then.
And so it was obvious that we just had to get rid of that attempt and just double down on high-skill legal talent and really leveraging them.

st.t: AI contracting: Deal velocity can undermine negotiation
st.an: Daniels supports AI-first delivery of completed contract work and faster deal execution, while treating speed as insufficient on its own. He emphasizes business context, lawyer-led judgment, quality preservation and unresolved redlining weaknesses, consistent with the cluster’s warning that deal velocity is not equivalent to quality-adjusted value.
qs: For contract negotiation, it sounds simple,  it's a legal negotiation, but we have to plug into a CRM and know who are the counter parties, what is the priority of this deal, what are the things that we have given on in the past for deals like this.
So like  you need a lawyer with some judgment on what is a court going to say in five years and we want it to get it right today.

st.t: Crosby delivery: Owning work enables workflow redesign
st.an: The source directly supports Crosby’s service-delivery model: it identifies Crosby as a law firm combining attorneys and AI, describes margin pressure as an incentive to redesign work, and presents company-specific business context as a potential technical advantage. Its evidence is founder testimony rather than independent proof of performance, and it does not substantively address human verification or agent-led negotiation.
qs: And we knew that we'd actually run the risk of being margin negative on some days of work, but the incentive would be really profound for everybody in the company to just rally around this goal of we need to find a more productive way to work.

For contract negotiation, it sounds simple,  it's a legal negotiation, but we have to plug into a CRM and know who are the counter parties, what is the priority of this deal, what are the things that we have given on in the past for deals like this.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Daniels supports AI-enabled redesign of contract delivery while retaining experienced lawyers for judgment-sensitive negotiation and accountability. Crosby’s proposed agentic workflow includes an auditable negotiation trail and human escalation rather than autonomous execution; its operational shift toward high-skill legal talent also reinforces the cluster’s caution about substitution. The capability remains prospective, consistent with the cluster’s view that evidence is early.
qs: So, if I know all the things you care about in a negotiation, when you're buying my software and I know all the things I care about, to just like simulate and show me an auditable trail of I would have asked for this and you'd responded with that, then I would have asked for this.
No, like at that point, then the human lawyers come in and then they talk through all those taste issues.

st.t: Expert workflows: Legal context becomes product infrastructure
st.an: Daniels supports the proposition that legal AI can create value in high-volume contract services by combining legal work with market benchmarks and client business context. His anticipated efficiency gain is based on an M&A anecdote rather than measured evidence, so the source reinforces an emerging workflow opportunity without establishing reliable transformation or end-to-end performance.
qs: And we inform that with market insights and benchmarks and all of your business context.
It was the wildest  conversation and I wish Crosby was around so that all of our AI lawyers could have gotten to the same conclusion much faster.

st.t: Repeatable services: Organisational redesign changes legal delivery
st.an: Daniels supports the proposition that AI-native delivery can organise legal expertise around repeatable, high-volume contract services informed by client and market context. His claim of faster legal deliberation is illustrative and counterfactual, however, rather than evidence of reliable performance or broader market transformation.
qs: We've identified like hundreds of contracts that are super high volume, super important, and like, you know, neglected today.
It was the wildest  conversation and I wish Crosby was around so that all of our AI lawyers could have gotten to the same conclusion much faster.

st.t: Startup scaling: Founder context can become bottleneck
st.an: Daniels supports the cluster’s proposition that founder intensity and context must be disciplined as a startup changes. He treats anxiety as motivating but says it should be channelled into constructive priorities rather than transmitted to the team. His customer-focused contract opportunity also aligns with organising the business around unmet client value, though he provides little evidence on delegation, decision rights or hiring practices.
qs: Every few months it feels like the company really changes.
Not come in and just be super anxious and freak everybody out, but just channel it cuz it's very motivating and it's a drive.

kp.k: Trusted advisers motivate a services-first AI business
kp.d: Daniels says conversations with 100-plus lawyers over a 9-month period helped shape Crosby as a legal services provider rather than solely software. Buyers sought trusted advisers, so Crosby aimed to meet that preference. He also reports discovering an alternative legal services market larger than legal software and growing four times as fast, without supplying market data or a measurement period.
qs: I think I probably spoke to 100 plus over a 9-month period
when people have some sort of legal issue, their instinct is to go to a trusted advisor.
And we saw that it's a bigger market for legal software and growing four times as fast.

kp.k: Per-document pricing aligns incentives with task automation
kp.d: Daniels describes eliminating hourly billing and charging by the piece of work to encourage lawyers and engineers under one roof to transfer tasks to agents. Crosby accepted the risk of negative margins on some work to create a strong productivity incentive. Although initially approaching large companies, it found immediate demand among startup founders. The claim that hourly billing always incentivizes inefficiency is the host's framing; Daniels explains Crosby's own incentive rationale.
qs: We had to have lawyers working with us, for us, under one roof.
if you do 10 tasks in an hour, 100 tasks in an hour, you're still billing an hour.
And bill by the piece of work we do.
we'd actually run the risk of being margin negative on some days of work

kp.k: Reported growth links contracting speed to client revenue
kp.d: In the later-recorded release addendum, Daniels announces a $60 million Series B and partnership with Lux to deepen negotiation research. He reports contracts representing over a billion dollars in client revenue since the June seed announcement, approximately 270 days, compared with about $20–30 million at that announcement. He reports speed improvements of 70–80% in some cases. These are founder-reported metrics, not Crosby revenue or independently substantiated performance measurements.
qs: We're announcing our $60 million series B
we closed contracts for our clients over a billion dollars in revenue for our clients since our seed announcement in June. So, that's like 270 days.
I think we'd done about 20 or 30 million maybe.
in some cases we've seen by like 70, 80%
With this round we're partnering with Lux for the first time.

kp.k: Contracting quality matters beyond immediate deal completion
kp.d: Daniels reports that client surveys identified responsive, thoughtful legal support as consequential for quarterly revenue targets because deals slip rather than usually disappear. He also says fundraising diligence exposed the importance of contract quality, leading Crosby to prepare for clients' subsequent fundraising reviews. No survey sample, method or quantified effect is provided.
qs: Having a really good, responsive, and thoughtful lawyer at your disposal is truly the difference between hitting your revenue goals this quarter or not.
And we did a lot of surveys and that's like the main factor. It just things slip. They don't usually die.
Investors start to diligence your company and look at your contracts and realize you guys are not buttoned up.

kp.k: Business context distinguishes counsel from generic contract review
kp.d: Daniels estimates that sales-agreement expertise is only 30–40% legal and 50–60% business context. Understanding products, technology, data storage, regulatory exposure and client risk preferences has shifted Crosby away from generic contract review toward an embedded combination of lawyers and agents. Interfaces should keep counsel informed as clients change insurance, features or data requirements.
qs: I would say only about 30 to 40% of the expertise is legal expertise.
And 50-60% is just about all the business context.
we're an extension of their business, not like an external service, but we feel embedded in their company as a mix of agents and lawyers.
we were missing at the beginning, where it was a generic contract review service.

kp.k: Context integrations constitute Crosby's proposed technical differentiation
kp.d: Daniels says Crosby depends on continuing foundation-model improvements and seeks to incorporate new models aggressively. Its own investment centers on scalable connections to clients' CRM, Slack and other information systems, supplying deal priorities, previous concessions, insurance and subprocessors at the appropriate workflow points. He regards this contextual integration as potentially defensible, rather than claiming proprietary foundation-model capability.
qs: If the models don't continue their improvements in every few months, we really see step function changes, then we're just like in slightly better law firm.
we have to plug into a CRM and know who are the counter parties, what is the priority of this deal, what are the things that we have given on in the past for deals like this.
We want to plug into your Slack and look at all the contexts in your sales channels.
figuring out exactly how to feed those into the right points is probably something we feel is like pretty defensible over time.

kp.k: An early staffing experiment favored experienced lawyers
kp.d: Daniels recounts testing whether AI could upskill relatively inexpensive offshore personnel and paralegals versus making experienced lawyers more productive. The former approach failed Crosby's quality expectations as contract volume increased. He and another lawyer handled hundreds of reviews while trying to preserve a 3-hour SLA, prompting a pivot toward high-skill lawyers during an approximately 2-month difficult period. This is a company-specific experience with its then-basic tools, not a general comparative study.
qs: Mostly paralegals and a lot of folks offshore.
And the quality bar was just not there
we really wanted to honor our like 3-hour SLA.
we were way more productive with just like the basic AI tools we built back then.
we just had to get rid of that attempt and just double down on high-skill legal talent and really leveraging them.

kp.k: Novel issues preserve demand for experienced human judgment
kp.d: At the original interview, Daniels reports approximately 12 lawyers and almost 10,000 sales agreements handled. Despite that accumulated work, unfamiliar issues arise at least two or three times daily, sometimes requiring a lawyer with 15 years of experience. His aspiration is to concentrate lawyers on these difficult judgments rather than routine work, while explicitly acknowledging Crosby has not reached that state. He also maintains that law school remains valuable.
qs: I think we have about 12 lawyers in this room
We've done almost 10,000 of them today.
It happens at least two or three times a day.
sometimes you do need a lawyer who has 15 years of experience
And our point to our lawyers is, this is all you should be doing.
We're not there yet
I tell people all the time, I think law school is still valuable.

kp.k: Software engineering offers an analogy for lawyers' future
kp.d: Daniels treats advances in code generation as a possible preview of legal AI, pointing to law's reliance on unstructured qualitative text. He reports unspecified data suggesting legal work could be second only to code generation in impact. Crosby's continued pursuit of excellent engineers despite AI coding capabilities illustrates his expectation that automation can coexist with demand for specialists making complex architectural or legal judgments.
qs: I do think it just provides us a bit of a window into where legal will go.
it seems like the service area second only to code gen where LLMs will have the biggest impact will be legal work.
we like fight like crazy to hire incredibly good engineers.
they make extremely complicated calls on our architecture and how we build things.

kp.k: Redlining remains a limitation and development priority
kp.d: Daniels characterizes legal LLMs as strong at precedent-based drafting and summarization, and reasonably capable at analysis and research, while describing redlining as insufficiently reliable. He suggests sensitivity to legally meaningful wording explains the difficulty. Crosby is prioritizing evaluation sets and lawyer-led data labeling to improve its redlining service; no named benchmark, score or error rate is supplied.
qs: they're really good at drafting brand new documents based on you've just given them much precedent.

kp.d: Daniels describes a goal of simulating negotiations using each party's preferences and producing an auditable sequence of offers and responses. He estimates a good prototype is probably a year away at the original interview, not an achieved capability. Human lawyers would still address judgment-sensitive issues after simulation and spend time directly negotiating matters important to the businesses rather than routine textual changes.

kp.k: Negotiation research inspires strategy but evidence is limited
kp.d: Daniels recalls research he thinks occurred at Stanford comparing two students with two agents in a simple stylized negotiation involving custody scheduling and supplied bottom lines. He reports agents achieved better outcomes for both parties every time within minutes, but supplies no citation, sample size or methods beyond that description. Separately, he reports a very limited internal study associating friendlier Word comments with greater acceptance of proposed changes; the suggestion that agents are less emotional comes from a host.
qs: we heard about research, I think at Stanford, that asked two students to do a negotiation
They would give the same bottom lines to two agents and have them simulate a negotiation.

kp.k: Efficiency work still contains expertise and judgment
kp.d: Drawing on an unnamed professional-services book, Daniels describes work maturing from expertise to experience to efficiency, using GDPR advice and eventual Big Four provision as an example. Crosby initially treated contracts as an efficiency opportunity, but Daniels now emphasizes embedded expertise, including frontier questions about AI data retention, liability and model ownership. Experienced lawyers' judgment and subtle drafting choices remain important even within high-volume work.

kp.k: Services spending offers a larger market than software
kp.d: Daniels contrasts approximately a trillion dollars in annual lawyer spending with legal-tech markets of about $18–20 billion, potentially approaching $30 billion, and estimates conservatively about $200 billion in contract-related legal work. These are unsourced market estimates. He sees an opportunity to redirect services spending toward AI, while predicting the top one or 200 US law firms will remain entrenched because their complex work is difficult to automate.
qs: that trillion-dollar amount that we spend on lawyers every year

I don't think the top one or 200 law firms are going anywhere anytime soon in the US.

I think there's conservatively about 200 billion that you spend on lawyers doing contract work, contract-adjacent work, reviewing and negotiating contracts.

kp.k: Lower prices could expand access and legal demand
kp.d: Invoking Jevons paradox, Daniels predicts cheaper legal services could expand the market rather than simply reduce spending. He estimates that 50 or 60% of Americans are neither poor enough for pro bono services nor wealthy enough to afford lawyers, and envisages new representation for eviction, employment and accident matters. This is an access-to-justice forecast with an unsourced population estimate, distinct from Crosby's reported enterprise contracting gains.
qs: there's this theory like Jevons paradox, which is the idea that as something gets cheaper, there's more demand for it.
there's probably about 50 or 60% of Americans who are not poor enough to qualify for pro bono legal services, but not wealthy enough to have access to lawyers.
They're not going to get evicted or fired or get a car accident without getting legal representation anymore.
We just see the market potentially expanding even as the cost of each piece of work goes down.

kp.k: Accessible explanations could empower clients beyond licensed tasks
kp.d: Daniels argues that AI summarization and context can make legal services less intimidating and less opaque. He distinguishes tasks needing licensed lawyers, such as court representation, from much legal-related work he believes need not require licensing. Responding to hosts' personal examples, he advocates empowering clients with information and retaining lawyers when needed, rather than stating a specific regulatory reform or rule interpretation.
qs: One of our missions is just making legal feel more accessible and less intimidating.
our clients should feel really confident in the work they're getting, and it should not be a black box.
there's just so much that's legal related that we don't have enough lawyers to do
we should have lawyers on hand when we really need them. But otherwise, you should be really empowered.

kp.k: Expansion depends on better redlining and negotiation infrastructure
kp.d: Daniels positions better redlining as the foundation for broader negotiation services, informed by market insights, benchmarks and business context. He envisages expansion from sales agreements to leases, lending and life-science agreements, saying Crosby has identified hundreds of high-volume, important, neglected contract types. This is a strategic ambition to become infrastructure for commercial agreements, not evidence that these broader services are already deployed.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Ryan Daniels predicts AI-led redesign of legal service delivery, centred on experienced lawyers working with agents, per-document pricing, context-aware contracting and eventually simulated negotiations. He also anticipates expanded demand rather than near-term disappearance of leading law firms.
pts.d:
1. Delivery model and incentives: Daniels argues that a legal services business, rather than solely software sold to lawyers, meets buyers' existing preference for trusted advisers. Bringing lawyers and engineers together and charging per piece of work creates incentives to transfer tasks to agents, although individual matters can initially be margin-negative. He describes discovering an alternative legal services market larger than legal software and growing four times as fast as part of the rationale for this choice.
2. Contract speed and commercial impact: Daniels reports that Crosby has accelerated contracting by 70–80% in some cases. He connects responsive legal services to whether clients meet quarterly revenue goals, saying that deals tend to slip rather than disappear. In the release-time addendum, he reports more than $1 billion in client revenue represented by contracts Crosby closed since its seed announcement—not Crosby's own revenue or a measured increment caused by AI.
3. Experienced-lawyer augmentation: Daniels says Crosby's early attempt to use AI to raise the quality of less-skilled contractors, principally paralegals and offshore personnel, did not meet its quality expectations. The company instead found experienced lawyers more productive with its tools and shifted to hiring highly skilled attorneys. His proposed model removes routine work while retaining human judgment, rather than eliminating lawyers.
4. Continuing need for legal expertise: Even after almost 10,000 sales agreements, Daniels says unfamiliar issues requiring lawyers arise two or three times daily. He expects lawyers increasingly to focus on these issues and on meaningful negotiation rather than mechanical edits. He argues that seemingly routine contracts still contain expertise- and experience-dependent work, including emerging questions about AI data retention, model ownership and liability.
5. Business context and explainability: Daniels estimates that sales-agreement work draws only about 30–40% on legal expertise and 50–60% on business context. He argues that effective AI-enabled counsel must integrate information about products, data, insurance, deal priorities and past concessions. He also says AI summarisation and contextual explanation can make legal services less intimidating and less opaque.
6. Relative model capabilities: Daniels predicts legal work could experience the largest LLM impact after code generation because it depends heavily on unstructured text. He describes models as strong at drafting from precedents and summarisation, and reasonably capable at analysis and research, but not yet sufficiently good at precise contractual redlining. Crosby's immediate ambition is to build the best redlining service through evaluation sets and lawyer-labelled data.
7. Agentic negotiation: Daniels's longer-term aim is to simulate exchanges between counterparties using their preferences and constraints, produce an auditable negotiation trail, and then have human lawyers address judgment-sensitive issues. This is not a prediction of immediate autonomous execution: he explicitly rejects simply signing the simulated result without lawyers' involvement.
8. Market structure and access: Daniels sees an opportunity to shift a large share of legal services spending to AI-enabled delivery. He estimates annual legal services spending at roughly $1 trillion and contract-related work at conservatively $200 billion. He nevertheless predicts that the leading 100–200 US law firms will remain because they are entrenched and perform complex work that is difficult to automate. He invokes Jevons paradox to suggest that cheaper services will bring previously unserved people into the market, potentially increasing total demand even as the cost of each matter falls.
9. Expansion beyond startup sales contracts: Daniels envisages applying better redlining and simulated negotiation to leases, lending and life-sciences agreements, including high-volume work currently neglected. He also anticipates greater user self-service for legal-related tasks, with lawyers available when needed, rather than licensed professionals performing every task.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is predominantly Daniels's account of Crosby's operations, customer research and experimentation, supplemented by unspecified benchmarks, market estimates and a secondhand account of negotiation research.
pts.d:
1. Delivery model and incentives: Daniels describes speaking with more than 100 lawyers over approximately nine months, observing buyers' preferences and investigating alternative legal services, including in India. He supplies no named market report for the relative size or fourfold growth claim. The pricing argument is an incentive-based explanation supported by his operating experience, not a controlled comparison.
2. Speed and impact: The 70–80% acceleration is an internal observation qualified as occurring in some cases; no baseline, sample, measurement method or breakdown of AI versus other process changes is supplied. Daniels refers to customer surveys when linking legal responsiveness to quarterly revenue timing. The addendum's contract-volume milestone is a company-reported traction measure and is not independent evidence of causal revenue uplift.
3. Staffing: Daniels gives a detailed operational anecdote: newly onboarded lower-skilled contractors did not achieve the expected quality gains, while he and another experienced lawyer processed hundreds of reviews using early tools. This is the stated basis for changing the staffing strategy; no formal comparative results are provided.
4. Human expertise: His basis is repeated encounters with novel clauses and legal questions during Crosby's contract work, reportedly after almost 10,000 agreements. The continued need for senior judgment is also illustrated by contractual AI-governance questions and anticipated future judicial interpretation.
5. Context and explainability: The percentage split between legal expertise and business context is his estimate from sales-agreement experience. He describes practical integrations with CRM, Slack and enterprise information tools as an operational improvement, but provides no quantified effect. Claims about explanation and user confidence are product judgments and aspirations.
6. Model capabilities: Daniels refers generally to data and legal and coding benchmarks without naming studies, benchmark sets, scores or tested models. His dissatisfaction with existing redlining products is based on personal trials. Lawyer data labelling and evaluation-set development are described as ongoing company work, not reported benchmark outcomes.
7. Negotiation: Daniels recounts research he thinks was at Stanford, involving a simple custody-scheduling negotiation between students compared with agents given the same bottom lines. He reports that the agents achieved better outcomes for both parties in minutes, but identifies neither the study nor methods and explicitly calls it stylised. This is a secondhand research claim he offers as inspiration, not demonstrated Crosby contract-negotiation performance. He additionally reports a very limited internal study associating friendlier Word comments with greater acceptance of proposed changes, without sample sizes or effect estimates.
8–9. Market and access predictions: Daniels supplies approximate market-size and unmet-need figures without sources. He estimates that 50–60% of Americans fall between eligibility for pro bono services and ability to afford lawyers. His demand-expansion forecast is a theoretical inference using Jevons paradox, not an observed population-level outcome. The protection of leading firms and expansion into other contract categories are his forecasts.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Daniels distinguishes current operational gains and limitations from a roughly one-year negotiation-prototype ambition; broader transformation depends on continuing model improvements, better redlining, adequate client context and human judgment.
pts.d:
The document is presented as a 2026 episode, but its main interview was recorded several months before the release-time addendum. Relative dates should therefore not be collapsed into one exact calendar date. The addendum places the $1 billion contract milestone about 270 days after the June seed announcement and describes research as a major focus for the following year.
Current or retrospective claims include selective contracting acceleration, the failed lower-skilled staffing approach, improved productivity with experienced lawyers, persistent novel legal issues and current weaknesses in model redlining. The staffing difficulty lasted roughly two months; Daniels does not claim that it proves AI can never upskill less-experienced workers.
Daniels says the company is probably a year away from a good agentic-negotiation prototype at the time of the main interview. Simulations depend on knowing both parties' priorities and would still be followed by human consideration of judgment-sensitive issues. He acknowledges that applying the stylised research idea to contracts has proved difficult.
The wider business thesis explicitly depends on models continuing to improve every few months. Without that improvement, Daniels says Crosby would be only a slightly better law firm. The integration strategy additionally depends on scalable access to client business information and supplying it at the appropriate workflow points.
Expansion into broader contract markets follows, in his account, successfully improving redlining. The access-to-justice forecast is conditional on legal costs falling; he provides no date for achieving it. His prediction that top firms will persist is qualified as 'anytime soon,' not permanent immunity. Human work concentrating exclusively on difficult questions remains an aspiration he says has not yet been achieved.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate beneficiaries are business clients and experienced commercial lawyers; the projected effects extend to traditional firms, alternative legal service providers and people currently unable to obtain legal help.
pts.d:
Business buyers: Startup founders, sales teams, in-house counsel and other corporate buyers would receive per-document rather than hourly services, faster contract turnaround, better explanations and advice informed by their business. Daniels connects this primarily to deal timing, revenue goals and fundraise diligence—not to evidence of improved public access to justice.
Experienced lawyers: Daniels's model retains skilled attorneys for unfamiliar law, strategic decisions, contextual judgment and negotiation with counterparties while agents take on more routine drafting and editing. Human involvement remains central both in current delivery and in the proposed simulated-negotiation workflow.
Paralegals and offshore contractors: They were the focus of Crosby's unsuccessful early upskilling experiment. Daniels reports a company-specific decision to favour experienced lawyers, not a profession-wide employment estimate or quantified displacement forecast.
Providers and vendors: Crosby positions itself as delivering legal work through an AI-first services business, distinct from vendors selling legal software. Daniels sees legal services spending as a much larger opportunity than software spending and cites the alternative legal services market as evidence of buyer openness to nontraditional delivery. He expects leading established US firms to remain resilient because of their complex work and entrenched relationships.
The public: Daniels anticipates that people unable to afford lawyers could obtain representation for eviction, dismissal and accidents if prices decline. He also envisages people using AI-supported information and self-service for routine legal-related needs, consulting licensed lawyers when necessary. These are prospective access and empowerment claims; Crosby's reported commercial-contract milestones do not demonstrate those outcomes.
Additional contract users: Tenants, lenders, life-sciences businesses and other parties to neglected, high-volume agreements are prospective users of expanded redlining and negotiation services, rather than established beneficiaries evidenced in the interview.
